organizations.normalization_notes: The Army biography identifies this 1941 command. NPS documents an intervening military-police assignment after Pearl Harbor, so K Company is not the immediate pre-COI posting.
The National Park Service explicitly names Eifler's pre-service federal employer; no modern successor is substituted.

claims.claim_text: Eifler commanded K Company, 35th Infantry Regiment, after his early-1941 call to Army active duty; this was not his final documented pre-COI assignment.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The Army biography identifies K Company. The NPS history adds a subsequent military-police command after Pearl Harbor before his 1942 COI assignment.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High: exact indexed full name and colonel rank match the Army biography, while NPS identifies the same distinctive Detachment 101 commander.
claims.temporal_assessment: Definitely pre-OSS, but superseded by the military-police and COI assignments; exact K Company end date unknown.
claims.match_notes: Revises the earlier immediate-pre-OSS interpretation without deleting the historic claim ID. The company remains a military unit, not a civilian employer.

claims.claim_text: Eifler's last documented civilian employer before his 1941 Army active-duty recall was the U.S. Customs Service, where he had become chief Customs Inspector in Hawaii in 1940.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: NPS explicitly identifies the U.S. Customs Service and the 1940 Hawaii appointment; the Army biography independently places his customs work before active-duty recall.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High: exact full name, customs-to-Army chronology, and Detachment 101 command align with the indexed colonel.
claims.temporal_assessment: The civilian-employer sequence is strongly date-bounded before active Army duty, but the exact Customs separation date is not documented.
claims.match_notes: NPS supplies the historically named organization; this is civilian federal employment, distinct from the subsequent Army and COI assignments.

claims.claim_text: After Pearl Harbor, Eifler commanded an unidentified U.S. Army military-police unit guarding enemy alien detainees in Hawaii before his COI assignment.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The NPS history places a Hawaii military-police command after his 35th Infantry command; the Army biography then dates assignment to COI in 1942.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High: NPS and Army accounts identify the same Eifler by name, Army service, and Detachment 101 command.
claims.temporal_assessment: Strongly date-bounded after December 1941 and before COI service in 1942; no exact unit name or assignment orders were reviewed.
claims.match_notes: Do not silently infer the formal military-police unit designation or treat this Army assignment as civilian employment.

claims.claim_text: Eifler's best-documented immediate institutional affiliation before OSS was the Coordinator of Information, to which he was assigned in 1942 while remaining an Army officer.
claims.evidence_paraphrase: The Army biography records Eifler's 1942 COI assignment. NARA documents that OSS succeeded COI on 13 June 1942.
claims.identity_match_assessment: High: the Army biography names Carl F. Eifler, matching the indexed colonel, and identifies his Detachment 101 role.
claims.temporal_assessment: Strongly date-bounded COI-to-OSS agency succession; no individual administrative transfer order or exact date was inspected.
claims.match_notes: This is a government assignment and agency chronology, not Eifler's last civilian employer. His Army commission continued concurrently.

research_attempts.query_text: Carl F. Eifler customs service Hawaii 35th Infantry military police COI; official Army NPS NARA review
research_attempts.research_notes: NPS documents an intervening Hawaii military-police command omitted from the earlier Army biography summary. The previously immediate K Company affiliation is reclassified as earlier military service; COI is the immediate institutional predecessor to OSS. NPS explicitly names the Customs Service as the last civilian employer. The original personnel file and individual transfer orders remain unreviewed.
